mcqs.question: Why does a real competing offer typically move a negotiation further than cited market data alone?
options: Market data is always inaccurate compared to a real offer
It changes the recruiter's internal framing from 'the candidate wants more' to 'we will lose this candidate at the current number'
Companies are legally required to match any disclosed competing offer
Recruiters cannot access market data themselves
mcqs.explanation: A competing offer converts an abstract ask into a concrete retention risk with a specific dollar figure attached, which is a much easier internal case for a recruiter to act on than citing third-party survey data.

mcqs.question: What's the core tactic for getting multiple offers to land in the same window?
options: Applying to every company on the exact same day
Only applying to companies with identical interview loop lengths
Waiting until you have one offer before applying anywhere else
Starting slower-moving, higher-priority companies first and deliberately staggering faster-moving companies to finish around the same time
mcqs.explanation: Since companies run loops at very different speeds, deliberately starting the slow, high-priority ones earlier and delaying faster ones is what brings offers into the same window — leaving it to chance rarely produces alignment.

mcqs.question: Why should you generally avoid telling a recruiter that their offer is your backup choice, even if it's true?
options: It removes your leverage and can reduce how hard the recruiter fights internally for you
It's illegal to rank offers when speaking to a recruiter
Recruiters are required to report this information to other candidates
It has no effect on the negotiation either way
mcqs.explanation: Signaling that you're ranked lower removes the urgency that drives a recruiter to advocate hard for you internally — the useful disclosure is the existence and size of a competing offer, not your private preference ranking.

mcqs.question: In the worked example, why does disclosing the exact competing number ($195k base) work better than a vague claim of outside interest?
options: It doesn't actually work better, vague claims are equally effective
A specific figure gives the recruiter's internal comp process something concrete to check against policy and act on
It's the only way a recruiter is legally allowed to respond
Recruiters only respond to numbers stated in writing
mcqs.explanation: A recruiter can take a specific number to their comp team or hiring manager and get a concrete answer on what's approvable, while a vague claim of outside interest gives them nothing actionable to bring back internally.

mcqs.question: What's the biggest risk of bluffing a competing offer that doesn't actually exist?
options: Nothing serious happens even if it's discovered
It only risks a smaller-than-hoped-for raise
A discovered bluff can rescind the current offer entirely, since it signals a willingness to lie before the working relationship has even started
It's a common and low-risk tactic recruiters expect
mcqs.explanation: Recruiters can sometimes verify claims, especially in tight-knit industries or for senior roles, and a caught bluff doesn't just fail to move the number — it can cost you the offer entirely, since it signals dishonesty before you've even started.

mcqs.question: Why do companies rarely match a disclosed competing offer exactly, dollar for dollar?
options: Recruiters are personally penalized for matching offers
It's illegal for two companies to pay identical comp
Matching exactly can create internal pay-equity issues by pushing the candidate meaningfully above others at the same level
Competing offers are always exaggerated by candidates
mcqs.explanation: Fully matching a specific external number risks creating a visible pay gap against existing employees at the same level, which is why companies typically close most, but not all, of the gap instead.
